meta.title: AI Is Exploding… So Why Are Stocks Starting to Look Weak?
meta.speakers: Kyle (host), Melvin, Martin, Vincent (Milk Road analysts)
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · rates vs AI growth · OpenAI $70B ARR · frontier concentration risk · agents vs SaaS · SpaceX/Meta moats · Micron preview

snapshot: Recorded Sept 29, 2026: the market closed red despite bullish AI news because the **10-year hit ~5.25%** (a 19-year high), oil stayed above $92 and PMI surged, raising Fed-hike fears.

OpenAI reportedly hit **$70B ARR** (from ~$45B a month earlier and $20B at end-2025), which the bulls read as proof demand is accelerating and the bears (Martin, Vincent) as a headline number without cost data.
Vincent's frontier-lab risk list: Anthropic's $518B infrastructure commitments, 25% of revenue from two customers, and venture-funded startups exposed to a rate-hike cycle.
Meta's enterprise platform and OpenAI's new always-on agent reopened the SaaS debate: Melvin expects a round-two selloff, Kyle and Vincent say SaaS survives and agents use existing software.
Kyle's long-term moat pick is SpaceX (infrastructure, chips, space-based compute); Meta's moat is distribution and trust; Martin says data and compute decide it.
Micron reports that night: Melvin models **$52.2B** revenue and 87.5% gross margin vs ~$51B consensus and wants more long-term agreements than last quarter's 16.
The panel splits on risk: Martin holds **20% cash** and is considering more de-risking; Melvin stays bullish despite macro; Kyle sees no drawn-out bear market.

themes.status: S&P / NASDAQ WITHIN ~5% OF HIGHS · SEPT 29, 2026
themes.title: Good growth data is bad news: yields at 19-year highs against AI revenue growth
themes.lead: The panel agrees the AI trade is strong but splits on whether yields and a narrow market force a correction.
bullets: Melvin: market closed red despite Nvidia's **$150B buyback**, Meta pushing Muse into enterprise and a SpaceX Starship milestone; the 10-year briefly hit ~5.25%, a 19-year high.
Oil held above $92, September flash PMI hit a 5-year high, Dallas manufacturing showed higher growth and inflation, and consumer spending and the labor market held up — all raise Fed-hike risk.
Fed officials said the AI buildout could cause near-term inflation (memory and laptops up ~20%); Melvin warns mortgage rates could approach 8% by next week.
Martin is more bearish: airlines, machinery, homebuilders and the Russell 2000 keep falling, so capex alone cannot lift everything; he holds 20% cash and may de-risk more.
Kyle: sentiment indicators are fairly bearish, not euphoric, despite prices near highs; he sees a market climbing a wall of worry.
Melvin argues Bessent has to bring yields down because the US must refinance almost $10T of debt this year and cannot do it at 7-8%; he also cites midterms as a reason policy favors a strong market.
Kyle cites Elon Musk and an unnamed Fed figure expecting GDP growth to double from 2% to 4% next year; he sees no 2022-style long bear market, only possibly a pullback.

quote.text: I think there's absolutely no way we can have a drawn out bear market at this pace of growth, because it's not just growth of capex, it is growth of revenues.

names.name: Nvidia (NVDA)
names.blurb: Announced a $150B buyback; stock hasn't moved on it.

themes.title: OpenAI's $70B ARR jump and the always-on agent launch
themes.lead: A $30B ARR add in about six weeks convinced Kyle the frontier-lab growth is real; Martin says revenue is only half the picture.
bullets: OpenAI ARR reportedly went from $20B at end-2025 to ~$45B a month earlier to **$70B**; enterprise is its fastest-growing B2B line, up more than 700% since July.
ChatGPT has 1.2B weekly users and over 2.5M businesses; Anthropic is roughly $75B and still growing, and Grok's agent product has likely added billions.
Kyle credits the spike partly to the Astra model (and Codex); Martin counters that Claude Sonnet 5.5, announced the day before, is 5x cheaper and more performant.
On Dev Day OpenAI launched *Dots*, an always-on agent in ChatGPT with its own cloud computer, browser and thousands of app connectors — Kyle calls it Grok's bot inside ChatGPT.
Kyle: Anthropic showed a profit last quarter and OpenAI is rumored to show one in Q3; he says profit matters less than growth right now.

Martin disagrees: revenue is easy to boost, training and inference costs are unknown, and an OpenAI product manager said subscription token usage will be cut because subscriptions are heavily subsidized.
Kyle expects new compute commitments on Dev Day, recalling last year's 6 GW AMD deal that sent AMD up 24%.
themes.watch: Kyle is a co-owner of Milk Road, which sells portfolio access; he says he uses Grok's agent heavily, while Martin and Vincent have been the bearish voices on OpenAI.

names.name: AMD (AMD)
names.blurb: Last year's 6 GW OpenAI GPU deal lifted it 24%; Kyle expects more such deals.

themes.title: Vincent and Martin's frontier-lab risk list, and Kyle's diversification rebuttal
themes.lead: The bear case is that compute demand rests on two heavily leveraged customers, while the bull case says new buyers diversify the demand.
bullets: Vincent: Anthropic's IPO numbers (via Reuters) show ~$518B of planned AI infrastructure spend, ~80% committed, which took a key risk off the table that day.
He flags that 25% of Anthropic's revenue came from two customers (end-2025 data); his guess is Microsoft and Cursor, and Cursor's integration into SpaceX could move that demand.
From a podcast he heard, ~25% of frontier AI revenue comes from venture-funded startups, which a rate-hike cycle could hit.
Vincent: with 40-60%+ of a portfolio in frontier-linked names, taking some chips off the table makes sense.
Martin cites SemiAnalysis: OpenAI and Anthropic could buy 40-50% of next year's new compute, so even the expectation of trouble could trigger a selloff.

Kyle's rebuttal: if SpaceX/xAI and Meta take a larger share, the buyers get bigger with other revenue (rocket launches, Starlink, a multi-hundred-billion-dollar ad business); Vincent agrees diversification is good but adoption of Meta's and xAI's agents is the unknown.
themes.watch: Vincent and Martin hold large AI allocations themselves; their warnings are partly portfolio-sizing advice.

themes.status: SOFTWARE DROPPED 3-4% ON META ENTERPRISE LAUNCH
themes.title: Agents versus SaaS: round-two selloff or buy the dip?
themes.lead: Melvin expects another software selloff as labs go after enterprise; Kyle and Vincent say agents will use existing software and SaaS survives.
bullets: Meta launched its enterprise platform and Muse push earlier that week; software stocks dropped 3-4% the day before, echoing the earlier selloff when Anthropic went after legal and financial services.
Melvin: seat-based models break when agents use Salesforce or ServiceNow on a person's behalf; he expects some names to be decimated again.
Kyle: more agents means more businesses and more SaaS needed; Salesforce's Agentforce is its fastest-growing product, built on usage, and Grok's bot now runs inside Slack.
Kyle adds the labs must build on the application layer rather than just resell tokens; the risk is that OpenAI or Anthropic rebuild SaaS tools in-house.
Martin's near-term worry: the market will group all software together and sell it, as earlier this year, and many stocks are still down 50-60% even among the good ones.
Vincent: agents are rational and the world is compute constrained, so they will use legacy software rather than rebuild it; he would buy the dip, and billions of agents will use existing tools.
Martin and Vincent argue Salesforce and ServiceNow are embedded data companies the labs cannot easily displace; Kyle counters that Claude and OpenAI are also integrated everywhere.

quote.text: SAS is not dead by any means. I think we need more SAS as a result of using agents.

names.name: Salesforce (CRM)
names.blurb: Agentforce is its fastest-growing product; agents run inside Slack.

names.name: ServiceNow (NOW)
names.blurb: Embedded workflow data company; exposed to the SaaS sentiment.

themes.title: Where the moat is: SpaceX's infrastructure, Meta's distribution and trust
themes.lead: As every lab converges on the full stack, Kyle backs SpaceX's physical moat, Melvin and Vincent back Meta's distribution, and Martin says data decides.
bullets: Kyle: labs can go up the stack to apps, or down to infrastructure as SpaceX and Meta are doing; SpaceX has the biggest moat via data centers, space-based compute and Terafab chip production.
An ARC analyst expects SpaceX to reach 66.6 GW of compute by 2031; Elon replied he would be disappointed if that were as low; SpaceX is at about 1.4 GW now.
Elon's end-of-year compute target rose from 2 GW to 2.6 GW, and concrete is already down for Terafab.
The Information reported Anthropic's SpaceX deal is worth up to **$84B**, up from an initial ~$45B, for terrestrial compute; Kyle says it was not priced in and SpaceX ran on it.
Martin: data is how companies differentiate (Figure, Eli Lilly, Bending Spoons, Tesla all chase data); Kyle adds you need both data and compute.

Meta: stock is up ~45% in two weeks; Vincent says the compute spend now has a clear agentic use; Melvin credits Zuckerberg for delaying Muse until it was trustworthy; both call distribution across Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook the edge.
Kyle laughs off Blue Origin's raise (reportedly ~15x oversubscribed, $150B valuation) as having no shot against Starship; Martin says it is a decade behind.
Kyle's anecdote: Siri failed a simple gram-to-pound conversion, while Grok is built into his Tesla — Apple and Google could still act, and Vincent says Apple's CEO has a tech background.
themes.watch: Melvin owns Meta; Kyle says Grok is built into his Tesla and he uses it daily, which colors his SpaceX/xAI enthusiasm.

themes.title: Micron preview: long-term agreements and the 'not cyclical' narrative
themes.lead: Everyone expects a blowout quarter; the debate is whether guidance, long-term agreements and 2028 supply can move the stock.
bullets: Wall Street expects ~$51B revenue and ~$30-31 EPS; Melvin's estimate is **$52.2B** with an 87.5% gross margin.
Melvin wants Micron to address new supply and China's memory makers, its HBM4 shipping pipeline, and more long-term agreements than last quarter's 16 to kill the cyclical narrative.

Kyle: earnings won't move the stock; the risks are guidance and OpenAI/Anthropic. Vincent disagrees and says the outlook matters, including the base revenue and margin inside the long-term agreements and 2028 supply.
A report says Samsung's customers want deals of 10+ years, to 2035-2036; Martin heard the whole Korean memory supply is locked in through 2031.
Vincent: locked-in pricing is tricky because it trades off a lower fixed price against flexible capacity at higher margins; Melvin says memory sells to profitable buyers, unlike neoclouds.
Martin wants memory companies to announce buybacks or dividends since they trade at cheap prices; Micron cannot buy back until December.

Melvin notes Nvidia's buyback is $150B of up to ~$250B over 18 months with no stock move yet; Kyle says that's slow pressure on a $5T stock; a UBS analysis said Micron could buy back ~40% of its float.
themes.watch: Melvin published a Micron note on the Milk Road Pro platform with his estimate, so his forecast is also a product call.

names.name: Micron (MU)
names.blurb: Reports Wednesday; Melvin expects a blowout, stock reaction a coin toss.

names.name: Nvidia (NVDA)
names.blurb: $150B buyback of ~$250B over 18 months used as a buyback-impact reference.

takeaways.title: Watch the 10-year and oil, not just AI headlines — the panel treats yields near 5.25% as the main near-term risk.
Size frontier-lab exposure against the concentration risks (two customers, venture-funded demand, 40-50% of compute) before adding.
Separate SaaS names with usage-based agent products from seat-based ones before buying the dip.
Read Micron's quarter through long-term agreement count, HBM4 and 2028 supply, not the headline beat.
Test the SpaceX and Meta moat claims against compute, data and distribution rather than model rankings.

hot_takes.take: I think there's absolutely no way we can have a drawn out bear market at this pace of growth.
Nobody cares about the number. All they need is a good UX and a good UI to run their business inside of these platforms and they'll pay the money.
hot_takes.why: Dismisses model quality and price as the driver of AI revenue.

hot_takes.take: I would bet it's not even profitable at this point.
hot_takes.why: Bearish call against a $70B ARR headline.

hot_takes.take: Software stocks are getting ready for a round two selloff... this is just going to decimate some of these software names once again.
The only person that's building for the biggest moat is SpaceX, Elon.
